<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|316|FUNCTION|}}</noinclude>if <math>n_1</math>, <math>n_2</math>, … <math>n_r</math> be positive integers, the rational function
{{block center|<math>\frac{1}{1-\zeta}\left\{1-\left(\frac{c_1-1}{c_1-\zeta}\right)^{n_1}\right\}</math>}}
is finite at <math>\zeta=1</math>, and has a pole of order <math>n_1</math> at <math>\zeta=c_1</math>; the rational function
{{block center|<math>\frac{1}{1-\zeta}\left\{1-\left(\frac{c_1-1}{c_1-\zeta}\right)^{n_1}\right\}\left\{1-\left(\frac{c_2-c_1}{c_2-\zeta}\right)^{n_2}\right\}^{n_1}</math>}}
is thus finite except for <math>\zeta=c_2</math>, where it has a pole of order <math>n_1n_2</math>; finally, writing
{{block center|<math>x_s = \left(\frac{c_s-c_{s-1}}{c_s-\zeta}\right)^{n_s}</math>,}}
the rational function
{{block center|<math>\text{U}=(1-\zeta)^{-1}(1-x_1)(1-x_2)^{n_1}(1-x_3)^{n_1n_2}\dots(1-x_r)^{n_1n_2\dots n_{r-1}}</math>}}
has a pole only at <math>\zeta=1+c</math>, of order <math>n_1n_2\dots n_r</math>.

The difference <math>(1-\zeta)^{-1}-\text{U}</math> is of the form <math>(1-\zeta)^{-1}\text{P}</math>, where P, of the form
{{block center|<math>1-(1-\rho_1)(1-\rho_2)\dots(1-\rho_k)</math>,}}
in which there are equalities among <math>\rho_1</math>, <math>\rho_2</math>, … <math>\rho_k</math>, is of the form
{{block center|<math>\Sigma\rho_1-\Sigma\rho_1\rho_2+\Sigma\rho_1\rho_2\rho_3-\dots</math>;}}
therefore, if <math>|r_i|=|\rho_i|</math>, we have
{{block center|<math>|\text{P}|<\Sigma r_1+\Sigma r_1r_2+\Sigma r_1r_2r_3+\dots<(1+r_1)(1+r_2)\dots(1+r_k)-1</math>;}}
now, so long as <math>\zeta</math> is without the closed curve above described round <math>\zeta=1</math>, <math>\zeta=1+c</math>, we have
{{block center|<math>\left|\frac{1}{1-\zeta}\right|<\frac{1}{a},\ \left|\frac{c_m-c_{m-1}}{c_m-\zeta}\right|<\frac{c/r}{a}<\sigma</math>,}}
and hence
{{block center|<math>|(1-\zeta)^{-1}-\text{U}|<a^{-1}\{(1+\sigma^{n_1})(1+\sigma^{n_2})^{n_1}(1+\sigma^{n_3})^{n_1n_2}\dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>(1+\sigma^{n_r})^{n_1n_2\dots n_{r-1}}-1\}</math>.}} Take an arbitrary real positive <math>\epsilon</math>, and <math>\mu</math>, a positive number, so that <math>\epsilon^\mu-1 < \epsilon a</math>, then a value of <math>n_1</math> such that <math>\sigma^{n_1} < \mu/(1+\mu)</math> and therefore <math>\sigma^{n_1}/(1-\sigma^{n_1}) < \mu</math>, and values for <math>n_2</math>, <math>n_3</math>, … such that <math>\sigma^{n_2} < \frac{1}{n_1}\sigma^{2n_1}</math>, <math>\sigma^{n_3} < \frac{1}{n_1n_2}\sigma^{3n_1}, \dots \sigma^{n_r} < \frac{1}{n_1\dots n_{r-1}}\sigma^{n_rn_1}</math>; then, as <math>1+x < e^x</math>, we have <math>|(-\zeta)^{-1}-\text{U}| < a^{-1}\{\exp\,(\sigma^{n_1}+n_1\sigma^{n_2}+n_1n_2\sigma^{n_3}+\dots+n_1n_2\dots n_{r-1}\sigma^{n_r})-1\}</math>, and therefore less than
{{block center|<math>a^{-1}\{\exp\,(\sigma^{n_1}+\sigma^{2n_1}+\dots+\sigma^{n_rn_1})-1\},</math>}}
which is less than
{{block center|<math>\frac{1}{a}\left[\exp\left(\frac{\sigma^{n_1}}{1-\sigma^{n_1}}\right)-1\right]</math>}}
and therefore less than <math>\epsilon</math>.

The rational function U, with a pole at <math>\zeta=1+c</math>, differs therefore from <math>(1-\zeta)^{-1}</math>, for all points outside the closed region put about <math>\zeta=1</math>, <math>\zeta=1+c</math>, by a quantity numerically less than <math>\epsilon</math>. So long as <math>a</math> remains the same, <math>r</math> and <math>\sigma</math> will remain the same, and a less value of <math>\epsilon</math> will require at most an increase of the numbers <math>n_1, n_2, \dots n_r</math>; but if <math>a</math> be taken smaller it may be necessary to increase <math>r</math>, and with this the complexity of the function U.

Now put
{{block center|<math>z=\frac{c\zeta}{c+1-\zeta},\quad \zeta=\frac{(c+1)z}{c+z};</math>}}
thereby the points <math>\zeta=0</math>, <math>1</math>, <math>1+c</math> become the points <math>z=0</math>, <math>1</math>, <math>\infty</math>, the function <math>(1-z)^{-1}</math> being given by <math>(1-z)^{-1}=c(c+1)^{-1}(1-\zeta)^{-1}+(c+1)^{-1}</math>; the function U becomes a rational function of <math>z</math> with a pole only at <math>z=\infty</math>, that is, it becomes a polynomial in <math>z</math>, say <math>\frac{c+1}{c}\text{H}-\frac{1}{c}</math>, where H is also a polynomial in <math>z</math>, and {{block center|<math>\frac{1}{1-z}-\text{H}=\frac{c}{c+1}\left[\frac{1}{1-\zeta}-\text{U}\right];</math>}}
the lines <math>\eta=\pm a</math> become the two circles expressed, if <math>z=x+iy</math>, by
{{block center|<math>(x+c)^2+y^2=\pm\frac{c(c+1)}{a}y,</math>}}
the points <math>(\eta=0,\ \xi=1-a)</math>, <math>(\eta=0,\ \xi=1+c+a)</math> become respectively the points <math>(y=0,\ x=c(1-a)/(c+a)</math>,<math>(y=0,\ x=-c(1+c+a)/a)</math>, whose limiting positions for <math>a=0</math> are respectively <math>(y=o,\ x=1)</math>, <math>(y=0,\ x=-\infty)</math>. The circle <math>(x+c)^2+y^2=c(c+1)y/a</math> can be written
{{block center|<math>y=\frac{(x+c)^2}{2\mu}+\frac{(x+c)^4}{2\mu}\{\mu+\sqrt{[\mu^2-(x+c)^2]}\}^{-2},</math>}}
where <math>\mu=\tfrac{1}{2}c(c+1)/a</math>; its ordinate <math>y</math>, for a given value of <math>x</math>, can therefore be supposed arbitrarily small by taking <math>a</math> sufficiently small.

We have thus proved the following result; taking in the plane of <math>z</math> any finite region of which every interior and boundary point is at a finite distance, however short, from the points of the real axis for which <math>1\leqq x\leqq\infty</math>, we can take a quantity <math>a</math>, and hence, with an arbitrary <math>c</math>, determine a number <math>r</math>; then corresponding to an arbitrary <math>\epsilon_s</math> we can determine a polynomial <math>\text{P}_s</math>, such that, for all points interior to the region, we have
{{block center|<math>|(1-z^{-1})-\text{P}_s|<\epsilon_s;</math>}}
thus the series of polynomials
{{block center|<math>\text{P}_1+(\text{P}_2-\text{P}_1)+(\text{P}_3-\text{P}_2)+\dots,</math>}} constructed with an arbitrary aggregate of real positive numbers <math>\epsilon_1</math>, <math>\epsilon_2</math>, <math>\epsilon_3, \dots</math> with zero as their limit, converges uniformly and represents <math>(1-z)^{-1}</math> for the whole region considered.

§ 12. ''Expansion of a Monogenic Function in Polynomials, over a Star Region.''—Now consider any monogenic function <math>f(z)</math> of which the origin is not a singular point; joining the origin to any singular point by a straight line, let the part of this straight line, produced beyond the singular point, lying between the singular point and <math>z=\infty</math>, be regarded as a barrier in the plane, the portion of this straight line from the origin to the singular point being erased. Consider next any finite region of the plane, whose boundary points constitute a path of integration, in a sense previously explained, of which every point is at a finite distance greater than zero from each of the barriers before explained; we suppose this region to be such that any line joining the origin to a boundary point, when produced, does not meet the boundary again. For every point <math>x</math> in this region <math>\text{R}</math> we can then write
{{block center|<math>2\pi if(x) = \int \frac{dt}{t}\, \frac{f(t)}{1-xt^{-1}},</math>}}
where <math>f(x)</math> represents a monogenic branch of the function, in case it be not everywhere single valued, and <math>t</math> is on the boundary of the region. Describe now another region <math>\text{R}_0</math> lying entirely within <math>\text{R}</math>, and let <math>x</math> be restricted to be within <math>\text{R}_0</math> or upon its boundary; then for any point <math>t</math> on the boundary of <math>\text{R}</math>, the points <math>z</math> of the plane for which <math>zt^{-1}</math> is real and positive and equal to or greater than 1, being points for which <math>|z|=|t|</math> or <math>|z|>|t|</math>, are without the region <math>\text{R}_0</math>, and not infinitely near to its boundary points. Taking then an arbitrary real positive <math>\epsilon</math> we can determine a polynomial in <math>xt^{-1}</math>, say <math>\text{P}(xt^{-1})</math>, such that for all points <math>x</math> in <math>\text{R}_0</math> we have
{{block center|<math>|(1-xt^{-1})^{-1} - \text{P}(xt^{-1})| < \epsilon;</math>}}
the form of this polynomial may be taken the same for all points <math>t</math> on the boundary of <math>\text{R}</math>, and hence, if <math>\text{E}</math> be a proper variable quantity of modulus not greater than <math>\epsilon</math>,
{{block center|<math>\left|2\pi if(x) - \int\frac{dt}{t}f(t)\text{P}(xt^{-1})\right| = \left|\int\frac{dt}{t}f(t)\text{E}\right| \leqq \epsilon\text{LM},</math>}}
where <math>\text{L}</math> is the length of the path of integration, the boundary of <math>\text{R}</math>, and <math>\text{M}</math> is a real positive quantity such that upon this boundary <math>|t^{-1}f(t)| < \text{M}</math>. If now
{{block center|<math>\text{P}(xt^{-1}) = c_0 + c_1xt^{-1} + \dots + c_mx^mt^{-m},</math>}}
and
{{block center|<math>\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int t^{-r-1}f(t)\,dt = \mu_r,</math>}}
this gives
{{block center|<math>|f(x) - \{c_0\mu_0 + c_1\mu_1x + \dots + c_m\mu_mx^m\}| \leqq \epsilon\text{LM}/2\pi,</math>}}
where the quantities <math>\mu_0</math>, <math>\mu_1</math>, <math>\mu_2</math>, <math>\dots</math> are the coefficients in the expansion of <math>f(x)</math> about the origin.

If then an arbitrary finite region be constructed of the kind explained, excluding the barriers joining the singular points of <math>f(x)</math> to <math>x = \infty</math>, it is possible, corresponding to an arbitrary real positive number <math>\sigma</math>, to determine a number <math>m</math>, and a polynomial <math>\text{Q}(x)</math>, of order <math>m</math>, such that for all interior points of this region
{{block center|<math>|f(x) - \text{Q}(x)| < \sigma.</math>}}
Hence as before, within this region <math>f(x)</math> can be represented by a series of polynomials, converging uniformly; when <math>f(x)</math> is not a single valued function the series represents one branch of the function.

The same result can be obtained without the use of Cauchy's integral. We explain briefly the character of the proof. If a monogenic function of <math>t</math>, <math>\phi(t)</math> be capable of expression as a power series in <math>t - x</math> about a point <math>x</math>, for <math>|t - x| \leqq \rho</math>, and for all points of this circle <math>|\phi(t)| < g</math>, we know that <math>|\phi^{(n)}(x)| < g\rho^{-n}(n!)</math>. Hence, taking <math>|z| < \tfrac{1}{3}\rho</math>, and, for any assigned positive integer <math>\mu</math>, taking <math>m</math> so that for <math>n > m</math> we have <math>(\mu + n)^\mu < (\tfrac{3}{2})^n</math>, we have {{block center|<math>\left|\frac{\phi^{(\mu+n)}(x).z^n}{n!}\right| < \frac{\phi^{(\mu+n)}(x)}{(\mu+n)!}(\mu+n)^\mu|z|^n < \frac{g}{\rho^{\mu+n}}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^n\left(\frac{\rho}{3}\right)^n < \frac{g}{\rho^\mu 2^n},</math>}}
and therefore
{{block center|<math>\phi^{(\mu)}(x+z) = \sum_{n=0}^{m} \frac{\phi^{(\mu+n)}(x)}{n!} z^n + \epsilon_\mu,</math>}}
where
{{block center|<math>\left|\epsilon_\mu\right| < \frac{g}{\rho^\mu}\sum_{n=m+1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^n} < \frac{g}{\rho^\mu 2^m}.</math>}}

Now draw barriers as before, directed from the origin, joining the singular point of <math>\phi(z)</math> to <math>z=\infty</math>, take a finite region excluding all these barriers, let <math>\rho</math> be a quantity less than the radii of convergence of all the power series developments of <math>\phi(z)</math> about interior points of this region, so chosen moreover that no circle of radius <math>\rho</math> with centre at an interior point of the region includes any singular point of <math>\phi(z)</math>, let <math>g</math> be such that <math>|\phi(z)|<g</math> for all circles of radius <math>\rho</math> whose centres are interior points of the region, and, <math>x</math> being any interior point of the region, choose the positive integer <math>n</math> so that <math>\frac{1}{n}|x| < \tfrac{1}{3}\rho</math>; then take the points <math>a_1=x/n</math>, <math>a_2=2x/n</math>, <math>a_3=3x/n</math>, <math>\dots a_n=x</math>; it is supposed that the region is so taken that, whatever <math>x</math> may be, all these are interior points of the region. Then by what has been said, replacing <math>x</math>, <math>z</math> respectively by <math>0</math> and <math>x/n</math>, we have<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
